processing: A baked green tea base is layered with fresh jasmine blossoms that are later sifted out, so the leaf keeps the scent but not the flower. The round is repeated, and the number of scentings varies by lot.
harvest_season: The base tea is usually picked in early spring and stored until the jasmine blooms in summer, when scenting takes place.
appearance_dry: Typically curled strands with plenty of visible white down, as the name suggests.
appearance_wet: Soft, tender green-yellow leaf and buds, as is typical of downy jasmine grades.
taste_profile: Fresh jasmine over a smooth, sweet green tea, clean rather than perfumed when well made.

brewing.notes: Water around 85 C keeps the base sweet. Stale or very hot brews turn bitter under the jasmine.

vintage_note: Jasmine tea is normally sold by grade and not by vintage: the spring base is scented in summer and reaches shops from then on. As with other scented greens, buy recent stock and drink it within a year or so, because the aroma fades.
description:
Yinhao, 'silver down', is a grade of jasmine green tea rather than a place: the name points to a base rich in downy tips. In Fuzhou it is one of the recognised kinds of jasmine tea, and it is the jasmine that appears on a widely repeated 2001 list of China's ten famous teas.

Its making follows the usual jasmine pattern. Baked green tea meets fresh flowers, drinks in their scent as they open, and then the spent blossoms are removed. Better lots repeat this more than once, which layers the scent into the leaf instead of sitting on top of it.

A good cup is sweet and clean, with the jasmine rising first and the green tea holding up underneath. The common mistake is boiling water, which brings up bitterness and flattens the flower.

The name is used loosely, and no single grade standard is shared by every seller. Look for real down on the leaf and a fresh flower smell rather than a sharp, synthetic one. Lots of petals in the tin are decoration and say little about scenting.
history:
Yinhao has no well-documented founding story of its own. It belongs to the Fujian jasmine tradition and is named among the kinds of Fuzhou jasmine tea, whose scenting craft entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2014.

Its wider fame owes much to a 2001 list of ten famous Chinese teas, attributed to American press reports, which gave jasmine a place through this tea.
